requests.answerToSource:
Half of V-8 is already true and was measured again on this round: a project created under a programme that carries a ladder gets exactly that ladder's gates, never both. What you saw is the other half: your sixteen projects were scaffolded BEFORE RBT carried a gate model, and a declared ladder deliberately does not rewrite projects that already exist (D-33.2 — dated gates and filed evidence would move under people's feet). So the gap is the MIGRATION, and it is accepted as such: an explicit act that moves an existing project onto its programme's ladder, adopting the milestones that already match and refusing to duplicate. Until it ships, `adopt` on PUT /api/v1/milestones binds your Gate A..F rows to the scaffolded ones by their predictable ids rather than adding to them.

Q-7, answered from the code you asked us to read: the OPEN RISKS tile counts `status === "Open" && type === "Risk"`, scoped to the projects the filter has selected, plus portfolio-wide items that carry no project. Your withdrawal of the implication was right.

requests.title: Governance quality signals on the portfolio page: decision latency, action ageing, gate cycle time, RAID review compliance, exception age
requests.observed: A PMO that cannot see its own throughput cannot improve it, and these five are the leading indicators of a programme quietly stalling.
requests.answerToSource: Closed, at your priority and with your constraint honoured: no new data entry, no migration, five clocks read from timestamps the book already keeps. Every one of them can say 'not measured' with a reason, because five new metrics are five new places to make the REQ-33 mistake — a programme that has closed no gates does not have a cycle time of zero and is not doing well. The median leads and the tail travels with it, your own sentence about a healthy mean and a two-year tail. Gate cycle time refuses to average a four-gate and a six-gate ladder and keeps each rung's own figure instead. None of the five carries a colour: nobody has agreed what 'too slow' means for your group, and a threshold chosen in our file would be exactly the fabrication you caught us at. Three things we found while building it are filed as REQ-45, REQ-46 and REQ-47 — read those before you read the metrics, because two of the five are unmeasurable on a real book today for reasons that are governance holes, not measurement bugs.

requests.title: A value dashboard for the executive: spend against case, benefits by status, overdue reviews, top risks by exposure, gates due, exceptions open
requests.observed: The portfolio view answers 'is it on time and on budget'; nobody can answer 'is it worth it'.
requests.answerToSource:
Closed. Six figures — spend against case, benefits by status, overdue reviews, top risks by exposure, gates due, exceptions open — every one of them assembled from the book with nothing typed, and every one able to say « not measured » with a reason. None carries a colour: no threshold for « too little benefit » has been agreed, and inventing one here is REQ-33 under a new name.

The figure we are most pleased with is the exceptions one, because it is a trap: a book with no tolerance set shows `—`, not « 0 open ». An empty exception register on a portfolio that has declared no limits is not a clean bill of health, and this is the only screen in the product that says so.

The snapshot extends `report_period` rather than inventing a second period. `report_snapshot` could not carry it — it is one row per project with fixed EV columns, and five of the six figures are portfolio aggregates with no project. Both new tables are append-only at the database, and the database itself refuses to store an unmeasured figure carrying a zero: `CHECK ((state = 'N' AND value IS NULL AND length(why) > 0) OR (state = 'measured' AND value IS NOT NULL))`. That constraint is REQ-33 written into the schema, and there is a test that inserts the forbidden row to prove the refusal.

Filing is refused if the period was closed on another day (409, naming both dates) and refused twice over (409, pointing at the restate path). Today's figures cannot be filed under March.

One caveat you will meet immediately: on a fresh book four of the six read as honest absences, because the demonstration book carries no business case at all. That is REQ-48, and it is a demonstration defect rather than a product one.

requests.answerToSource: Confirmed, and worse than you filed it. On a book of budget-less projects the tile read ON TRACK 100%, SCHEDULE INDEX 1.00, COST INDEX 1.00; it now reads '—', '0 green · 0 amber · 0 red · N not measured', '—', '—'. Two things your report could not see. First, correcting the guard alone would NOT have fixed the tiles: with every project unmeasurable the live set is empty and the roll-up's own `: 1` fallbacks kept returning 1.00 — the page would have gone on lying. Second, and this is the one that matters: the manufactured green was being written into report_snapshot at period close, which is append-only by database rule, so it became permanent, unamendable history. We reproduced that in one API call. Your criterion is met on every surface we could find — page, print, Markdown export, dataset export, evidence pack, the frozen period, and the meeting pack — and the fourth state cost no schema change. 'Too early to measure' stays distinct from 'nothing to measure': both are absences, and neither is green.

history.note: Raised from the consolidated field report and worked by the full committee.

requests.title: A write refuses a body it does not understand, and writes no audit row for an act not performed
delivered: server/src/openapi.js (additionalProperties: false — the contract states the rule the server enforces)
requests.answerToSource: Delivered on the v1 half. The refusal names what the collection does accept and points at the contract; a refused body reserves no idempotency key, opens no transaction and audits nothing. Two latent faults fell out of building it: `decisions` asserted `version` without declaring it (so refusing it would have broken the REQ-15 round trip), and `business-case` had never had a described body in the published document because the collection matcher did not match a hyphen. The SESSION half — your PATCH /projects/:id/health returning 200 and auditing 'status returned to automatic', and POST attendance with the wrong key deleting every attendance row inside a frozen minute — is surveyed and not yet built: 89 mutating routes, 415 named field reads, and the design is written down (a declaration table plus one `r.use()` per router). It is the next thing on this line.

history.note: Raised from the consolidated field report and worked by the full committee.

requests.title: A rollout wave is one row per site, and the refusal says so and says where phases go
delivered: server/migrations/044_wave_is_a_site.sql (the constraint named, with its intent as a comment)
requests.answerToSource: Declined as a defect, and answered as a message — with your own fallback clause declined too, with reasons. It is design: rbac.js calls it 'the rollout wave per site', docs/14 V-06 says 'one row per site per rollout', the screen reads 'Sites in this rollout' and 'N live of M', and a test has held it since V-06. Your fallback asked us to remove `seq` if that were so — we decline: `seq` orders the SITES, the screen sorts on it and an index exists to serve that order; removing it would delete the order of the rollout to fix a message. What was wrong was the message. It now reads: 'a wave IS a site in this rollout, and seq is the order the sites go live in, not a phase number within one site. Record phases at a single site as milestones on the project.'

history.note: Raised from the consolidated field report and worked by the full committee.

requests.title: A decision may cite evidence that lives in a repository, not only at an http address
requests.answerToSource: Nineteen of your decision records went in with an empty evidence link because the true evidence could not be expressed, and that is the kind of silence a governance record must not cause. A repository path with a revision, a path at a commit, a bare commit and a named locator (git:, repo:, commit:, artifact:, run:) are now accepted alongside http(s). Prose is still refused, and deliberately: your own D-10 is the argument for it — a 200 on a body the route did not understand teaches the caller they wrote something. A sentence with no locator cannot be found again, and is not evidence.

history.note: Raised from the consolidated field report and worked by the full committee.

requests.title: The exception sweep can be asked for, not only waited for
delivered: server/src/index.js (a first pass at start, not only the hourly tick)
web/src/views/index.js (a Check now control where exceptions are read)
requests.answerToSource: You set a one-day tolerance, slipped four months and saw exceptions: [] throughout, because the sweep runs on an hourly interval with no first pass and no way to trigger it — so nothing could be observed inside a session. A control nobody can watch work is a control nobody can believe. It stays a constat, not a decision: it opens only what the numbers already say, it is audited under 'system', asking twice does not stack, and the authority to ask is the level that sets the margins.

history.note: Raised from the consolidated field report and worked by the full committee.

requests.title: A gate records when it was passed, whether or not it carried acceptance criteria
remaining: A gate marked done records the day it was marked and by whom, independently of whether criteria were attached; existing rows are not back-dated.
requests.observed: Measured while building REQ-28: `routes/portfolio.js` writes `milestone.accepted_on` ONLY when the milestone carries acceptance criteria. A gate ticked done without them gets `done = true` and no date at all — 24 of 24 gates on the shipped demonstration book. Gate cycle time therefore reports 'not measured' on a book where twenty-four gates have visibly been passed. The metric is telling the truth; the product cannot say WHEN most gates were passed, and that is a governance hole rather than a measurement bug.
requests.answerToSource: Filed against ourselves. This is the reason one of your five signals reads `—` on a real book, and we would rather you heard it from us than measured it.

history.note: Opened by the measurement counsellor while delivering REQ-28 — found in our own product, not filed by RT365.

requests.title: The RAID register records that a review happened, not only when the next one is due
remaining: A review is an event with a date and a reviewer; the next-due date is derived from the last one rather than replacing it.
requests.observed: `raid_item.review_on` holds the NEXT review date, and performing a review moves it forward — which erases the only evidence there was. Review compliance is therefore statable today and unstatable for last month, on any book. Of the five governance signals it is the one with no history at all, and its trend correctly reports that there is none.
requests.answerToSource: Filed against ourselves while delivering REQ-28.

history.note: Opened by the measurement counsellor while delivering REQ-28 — found in our own product, not filed by RT365.

requests.title: A decision records when it was ratified, not only that it was
remaining: decision_record.ratified_on, written when the status becomes Ratified; existing ratified rows keep a null date rather than a fabricated one.
requests.observed: Migration 039 gave a decision a status (Proposed → Ratified) and a ratifier, and no ratification date. So 'how long does ratification take in this programme' cannot be asked at all, and decision latency has to report proposed-but-unratified decisions as a note beside the number rather than counting them. One nullable column opens it.
requests.answerToSource: Filed against ourselves while delivering REQ-28.

history.note: Opened by the measurement counsellor while delivering REQ-28 — found in our own product, not filed by RT365.

requests.title: The demonstration book carries a business case, so the value and ranking screens are not empty on first run
remaining: A fresh `npm run seed` produces a book where some projects carry a business case and some deliberately do not, so both the ranking and the not-placed worklist are visible; and the suites that assert on the seeded book are made robust to it rather than adjusted to fit it.
requests.observed: The seed writes NO business case at all. So REQ-20 (the case), REQ-22 (its reconfirmation) and REQ-24 (the ranking) all open empty on a fresh book: RT365 would meet their own highest-priority request as a blank table of twelve rows saying what each of them lacks. Attempted in this round and REVERTED: six seeded cases turned 19 tests red, because several suites are written against a seed with no case — `case.test.js` relies on PRJ-101 having none, and `prioritise.test.js` asserts a top-two ordering that only holds on an otherwise-empty ranking. Those tests are not wrong; they are correct against the book they were written for. Editing nineteen of them to accommodate a demonstration improvement is the wrong way round.
requests.answerToSource: Filed against ourselves. You will open the ranking empty on a fresh book, and that is a demonstration defect rather than a product one — every row correctly says which input it lacks. It is worth doing properly, which means making the suites independent of the seed first and seeding the cases second.

history.note: Opened after an attempt in this round was reverted rather than paid for with nineteen test edits.

requests.title: A decision recorded through the session route is held to the same segregation of duties as one written through the contract
remaining: `POST /api/decisions` and the occurrence route resolve the ratifier in the directory and apply `canRatifyDecision` exactly as the contract door does; the screen's decision form offers a person rather than a text box; the refusal says who may ratify and why it is not the person who took or recorded it.
requests.observed: `POST /api/decisions` accepts `ratifiedBy` as free text — `String(b.ratifiedBy).slice(0,200)`, no directory lookup, no independence check — while `PUT /api/v1/decisions/:externalId` has enforced `canRatifyDecision` (H-3) since the security round. Before REQ-47 that was a soft hole: an unchecked NAME beside a status. REQ-47 made it materially worse, and we made it worse ourselves in the same release — the same route now writes `ratified_on`, so the unchecked claim is DATED and feeds a governance metric. A ratification nobody independent ever saw is now measurable evidence of a ratification.
requests.answerToSource: Filed against ourselves, and we are telling you before you measure it. It is not closed: closing it properly changes an authority rule and the decision form, and a hurried change to an authority rule at the end of a wave is how the check ends up weakened rather than applied. It is the first thing in the next wave.

history.note: Opened by the instrument counsellor while delivering REQ-45/46/47 — found in our own product.

requests.title: A human can ratify a decision from a screen, not only through the integration contract
remaining: A session route that ratifies a decision under the same independence rule, and an authority expression for portfolio-wide decisions.
requests.observed: The only door that moves a decision from Proposed to Ratified is `PUT /api/v1/decisions/:externalId`, because H-3 put the segregation-of-duties rule on that path. With `ratified_on` now recorded, a programme kept entirely by hand can never produce a ratification latency at all — the metric exists and their book structurally cannot feed it.
requests.answerToSource: Filed against ourselves while delivering REQ-47. It is a governance decision, not a field, so it is put down rather than guessed at.

history.note: Opened by the instrument counsellor while delivering REQ-45/46/47 — found in our own product.

requests.title: The write contract can record that a RAID review happened, not only move the date it is next due
remaining: A contract route for the review event, its OpenAPI entry, and its declared write body.
requests.observed: `PUT /api/v1/raid/:externalId` sets `review` directly, which is scheduling and is correct. There is no contract door for the review EVENT that migration 050 introduced. So an integrator syncing a real register can move the due date but cannot tell us a review occurred — which is precisely the defect REQ-46 just fixed for the screen, one door along.
requests.answerToSource: Filed against ourselves the moment 050 landed, rather than waiting for you to measure the asymmetry as you did with REQ-18.

history.note: Opened by the instrument counsellor while delivering REQ-45/46/47 — found in our own product.

requests.title: A gate's own list of what it watches is checked against the product, so a thing it does not name is reported rather than unseen
delivered: server/test/persistence.test.js (every table is cleared or declared kept)
requests.measure: server/test/persistence.test.js — it found `case_reconfirmation` on its first run
remaining: The same check for `scripts/audit/route-match.mjs` (its router map) and `scripts/audit/crud-audit.mjs` (its entity map): a router or table absent from those is invisible to F1 and F2, which is the gate lying in the safe direction.
requests.observed: This repository keeps five hand-written lists of things the product owns — F1's router map, F2's entity map, and reset-book's keep/clear pair — and every one shares a blind spot: a thing the list does not name is not reported missing, it is simply not seen. That has cost four releases in this round alone (`signals`, `ladder`, `valuepage`, `prioritisation_weighting`). reset-book's was the worst: its guard fires only at reset time AND only when the forgotten table holds a row, so a production book that had stored a value page could not be reset at all and no suite noticed.
requests.answerToSource: Filed against ourselves, half-closed in the same breath. The reset-book half is done and the test that closes it found a SECOND instance on its first run — `case_reconfirmation`, from REQ-22's work, which meant a book with a reconfirmed business case could not be reset either. Nobody had reported it because no suite reconfirms and then resets. That is the argument for checking the class rather than the instance, and the same argument is now owed to F1 and F2.

history.note: Opened and half-closed in the same round; the test found a second instance immediately.

channel.rule: issue #n = improvement I-n = REQ-0n; the Product Owner answers on the issue and closes it when the line is done
channel.counterpart: RT365 Program Orchestrator (docs/PMO.md); RT365 Product Owner agent decides on its side

acceptance.done: on the branch with its test
acceptance.accepted: the requester said so on the issue
acceptance.notAccepted: the requester is in a position to answer and has not — silence, or an objection not yet filed
acceptance.cannotAnswerYet: accepted is null: nothing is delivered to try, or the requester has said it cannot judge the line until it adopts the feature (E-9)

channel.escalation: a rejected refusal or done goes back to open with the objection quoted; the sponsor of both repositories is the tie-breaker

cadence.routine: Meridian Product Owner — RT365 field-return round
cadence.quietRound: a round that finds nothing new changes nothing and says so

release.state: The default branch carries 5.9.0 (77c4b49). Every improvement REQ-01..REQ-47 lives on claude/meridian-rt365-feedback-d6vo3i, which is 14 commits ahead and 0 behind — a fast-forward with no conflicts. Newest tag on the remote is v5.9.0; 5.10.0 through 5.14.0 exist only on the branch.
release.consequence: 28 requests in this register read `done` or `partial`, and the files they name do not exist for anyone who clones. `released` is therefore false on every line, and honestly so.
release.gate: scripts/audit/register-reachable.mjs (F12) counts this on every `npm run audit` and fails a tag build that claims otherwise.
release.whatIsNeeded: A maintainer merges the branch to main and pushes the tag. The owner AUTHORISED the merge on 08/09; it was then refused by the agent session's own permission classifier — `git merge --ff-only`, `git push origin <branch>:main` and even a local `git tag -a` (D-33.50). Pushing a tag ref is separately refused HTTP 403 by the session credential (D-33.18, D-33.30). Two different boundaries, neither routed around.
